title: Horvitz–Thompson Estimation and Unequal Inclusion Probabilities
engineName: The Horvitz–Thompson estimator weights each observed unit by the inverse of its chance of selection.
objectives: Define first- and second-order inclusion probabilities and distinguish them from draw probabilities.
Construct the Horvitz–Thompson estimator of a finite-population total.
Compute and interpret the design variance and its unbiased estimator when pairwise inclusion probabilities are positive.
Diagnose when an unbiased variance estimator cannot be computed from the observed sample.

prereq.name: Finite-population total
prereq.why: The target is the fixed sum of all unit values, not a superpopulation expectation.

prereq.name: Indicator variables
prereq.why: A unit contributes to the sample total only when its inclusion indicator equals one.

prereq.name: Expectation and variance
prereq.why: Unbiasedness and design variance are expectations over the random sampling design.

traps: The inclusion probability πᵢ is the probability that unit i appears in the final sample; it is not necessarily the probability of a particular draw sequence.
The HT estimator is a total estimator. Divide by N to estimate a population mean when N is known.
Design-unbiasedness does not mean every realised estimate equals the population total.
The variance estimator needs second-order inclusion probabilities πᵢⱼ; positive first-order probabilities alone are not enough.
If πᵢⱼ=0 for a pair, the usual unbiased HT variance estimator has an unavailable denominator and cannot estimate that pair's contribution.
An unbiased estimator of a nonnegative variance can itself be negative for a realised sample.
howto: Work in this order: define the target total, write each unit's inclusion probability, form the inverse-probability weighted total, and only then discuss variance. Keep πᵢ (one unit) separate from πᵢⱼ (a pair). In the worked SRS example, calculate every possible sample so the sampling distribution and variance are visible. The June 2026 PYQ anchor tests the distinction between an estimator, its variance estimator and the signs those quantities can take.

scenes.title: Three tools before the estimator
scenes.objective: Refresh finite-population totals, indicators and design expectation.
body: A finite population contains N fixed units with values y₁,…,y_N. The total Y=Σyᵢ is fixed. Randomness enters because the sampling design chooses which units are observed.
For each unit, define Iᵢ=1 when it is selected and Iᵢ=0 otherwise. Then the sample can be described algebraically without listing every possible sample.
The expectation Eₚ is taken over repeated samples generated by the stated design. It is not an expectation over changing population values.

items.recall: Y=Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ yᵢ, the sum of the fixed values of all population units.
refresh: The population is treated as fixed for design-based inference. Each unit has a value yᵢ.
Add the values of all N units to obtain Y. Sampling does not change Y; it only determines which values are observed.
A sample statistic is random because the selected set changes from one repetition of the design to another.

items.ask: What does the indicator Iᵢ record?
items.recall: Iᵢ=1 if unit i is included and 0 otherwise.
refresh: An indicator turns an event into a number. It is one when the event happens and zero when it does not.
For sampling, the event is 'unit i is in the final sample'.
The expected value of an indicator is the probability of its event, so Eₚ(Iᵢ)=Pₚ(i∈s).

items.recall: The expectation of the estimator over repeated samples under the design equals the fixed target.
refresh: Imagine repeating the same sampling procedure many times from the same finite population.
Each sample gives an estimate. The design expectation is the probability-weighted average of those estimates.
An estimator is design-unbiased for Y when that average equals Y. A particular sample estimate can still be above or below Y.

ask.q: Why is a realised sample estimate allowed to differ from the population total even when the estimator is unbiased?
ask.nudge: Unbiasedness is a statement about the average over the sampling design, not an equality for each sample.

scenes.title: Correct for unequal chances of selection
scenes.objective: Build the inverse-probability weighting idea before writing the estimator.
body: Suppose a survey deliberately samples some units more often than others. A raw sample sum over-represents units with high selection chances. The correction is to give a selected unit more weight when its chance of inclusion is small.

A unit selected with probability 1/2 represents two population units in the weighted total. A unit selected with probability 1 represents itself. The weight is the reciprocal of the unit's inclusion probability.

scenario.teaser: A small business survey oversamples large firms.
scenario.title: Why the weights differ
body: A regional business register contains small and large firms. The survey design gives every large firm a high chance of selection because large firms account for a substantial share of employment, while small firms are sampled at a lower rate. The survey analyst wants the total number of employees across all firms, not merely the total among respondents. Adding respondent counts directly would let the high-probability large firms dominate twice: they have larger employment values and they are more likely to appear. Inverse-probability weighting corrects the selection part of that imbalance. It does not change the observed employment value; it changes how much population representation that observation carries.
scenario.q: If a sampled firm has inclusion probability 0.20, what is its HT weight?
scenario.answer: 1/0.20=5. It represents five units' worth of inclusion weight in the estimator.

ask.q: What should happen to the weight when a unit's inclusion probability decreases?
ask.nudge: The weight is the reciprocal of the inclusion probability.

scenes.title: Read the sampling distribution
scenes.objective: Interpret how different samples produce different HT estimates.

viz.caption: The three possible size-two samples from a population of three produce HT totals 45, 60 and 75 under SRSWOR.

body: Take three population values 10, 20 and 30. Under simple random sampling without replacement of size two, every pair has probability 1/3. Each unit has first-order inclusion probability 2/3.
The HT estimate for a selected pair is the sum of its observed values divided by 2/3. The possible estimates are 45, 60 and 75. Their average is 60, the true population total.
The spread of these estimates is the design variance. A single estimate is not expected to equal 60 every time.

ask.q: What is the HT estimate for the sample containing units with values 10 and 30?
ask.nudge: Each selected unit has inclusion probability 2/3; divide each observed value by 2/3 before adding.

scenes.title: Inclusion probabilities and the HT total
scenes.objective: Define πᵢ and derive the estimator.

blocks.body: πᵢ=Pₚ(Iᵢ=1)=Pₚ(i∈s). For an estimable finite-population total, require πᵢ>0 for every population unit.
When N is known, the HT estimator of the population mean is ȳ_HT=Ŷ_HT/N. Do not divide by the sample size n.

flow.title: Build the HT estimator
flow.alt: Start with the target population total, identify each unit's inclusion probability, weight selected values by its reciprocal, and add them.
flow.note: Every unit must have positive first-order inclusion probability.

ask.q: Which quantity is divided by N to obtain the HT estimator of the population mean?
ask.nudge: First construct the estimator of the total; then divide that total estimate by the known population size.

scenes.title: Worked example: three units, sample size two
scenes.objective: Compute all possible HT estimates and the design variance.
scenes.problem: A population has y=(10,20,30). Draw an SRSWOR of size 2 from N=3. Find πᵢ, the HT total for each possible sample, the design expectation and the design variance.

steps.say: The true population total is the sum of all three fixed values.
steps.why: This is the target against which the design expectation is checked.

steps.say: Each unit appears in two of the three equally likely samples.
steps.why: There are three possible pairs and each is selected with probability 1/3.

steps.say: For sample {1,2}, weight both observed values by 1/(2/3).
steps.why: The HT total uses inverse inclusion probabilities, not the raw sample sum.

steps.say: Repeat for the other two possible samples.
steps.why: The estimates vary because the selected pair varies.

steps.say: Average the three estimates using their design probabilities.
steps.why: The design expectation equals the finite-population total.

steps.say: Compute the variance around the design expectation.
steps.why: Variance is the mean squared deviation of the estimator across all possible samples.

scenes.after: The estimator is unbiased even though none of the three possible samples has to reproduce the population values unit by unit. Always list the design's possible samples when a small exact example is given.

ask.nudge: It is the average squared deviation of the three possible estimates from their design mean of 60.

scenes.title: Pause and retrieve
scenes.objective: Recall the core definitions before the variance estimator.
scenes.intro: Answer first, then reveal the one-line definition.

items.a: The first-order probability that unit i is included in the final sample.

items.q: What is the HT contribution of selected unit i?
What condition makes the HT total identifiable for every unit?
What is the HT mean estimator when N is known?
Does unbiasedness force every sample estimate to equal Y?
items.a: No. It forces the design expectation to equal Y.

scenes.title: Complete the derivation
scenes.objective: Rebuild the unbiasedness proof one line at a time.
scenes.problem: Show that the HT estimator is design-unbiased for the finite-population total.

blank.hint: A unit contributes only when its inclusion indicator is one.

steps.why: The indicator representation lets us take design expectations.

steps.say: Use linearity of expectation and the inclusion probability.

blank.hint: The expected value of an indicator equals the probability of its event.

steps.why: This is the definition of first-order inclusion probability.

steps.say: Substitute and simplify the factor for each unit.

blank.hint: The denominator is the same positive inclusion probability.

steps.why: The weighting exactly cancels the expected inclusion indicator.

blank.hint: This was the target defined in the foundation scene.

steps.why: The design expectation equals the fixed total.

scenes.after: The proof is a four-step chain: indicator form → expectation → cancellation → target total.

scenes.title: Second-order probabilities and variance estimation
scenes.objective: Distinguish πᵢⱼ from πᵢ and state the unbiased variance estimator.

blocks.body: πᵢⱼ=Pₚ(i∈s and j∈s). For i=j, πᵢᵢ=πᵢ. For distinct units, πᵢⱼ describes their joint inclusion.
V̂ₚ(Ŷ_HT)=Σᵢ∈sΣⱼ∈s [(πᵢⱼ−πᵢπⱼ)/πᵢⱼ] (yᵢ/πᵢ)(yⱼ/πⱼ), when the required πᵢⱼ are positive.

blocks.h: A first-order condition is not enough
blocks.body: πᵢ>0 permits estimation of the total. The usual unbiased variance estimator also needs πᵢⱼ>0 for the pairs whose contributions must be estimated. A design that never selects a particular pair has πᵢⱼ=0 and the displayed estimator cannot recover that pair's contribution from the sample.

ask.q: What additional probability is needed to estimate the variance of the HT total?
ask.nudge: It describes the event that two specified units are both included.

scenes.title: Guided practice: compute the HT variance estimate
scenes.objective: Use pairwise inclusion probabilities for an SRSWOR example.
scenes.problem: For the population y=(10,20,30), N=3 and SRSWOR n=2, use the HT variance estimator to obtain its value for each possible sample.
hints: Write πᵢ=2/3 and, for distinct units, πᵢⱼ=1/3.
Substitute into the double-sum estimator; include both diagonal and off-diagonal terms.
For each sample, use the two selected units and their HT weights 15, 30 or 45.
scenes.answer: For samples {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, the unbiased variance estimates are 75, 300 and 75 respectively. Their average is 150, the true design variance.
scenes.check: The average of the variance estimates over the three equally likely samples must equal 150. If it does not, check the off-diagonal terms and remember that the double sum includes both (i,j) and (j,i).

scenario.teaser: A survey team must report uncertainty, not just a weighted total.
scenario.title: Can the variance be estimated from this design?
body: A field team uses a fixed-size design in which every unit has a positive chance of selection. The analyst can therefore calculate an HT estimate of the total. The team now asks for a design-unbiased estimate of its variance. That is a separate question. The analyst must inspect the pairwise inclusion probabilities, because the variance depends on joint inclusion as well as individual inclusion. If some pair can never appear together, its joint inclusion probability is zero. The total estimator can remain unbiased while the usual unbiased variance estimator is unavailable. Reporting a standard error without checking this condition confuses two different requirements.
scenario.q: Does πᵢ>0 for every unit automatically guarantee the usual unbiased HT variance estimator is available?
scenario.answer: No. The required pairwise inclusion probabilities must also be positive.

solution.say: Under SRSWOR, each unit is in 2 of the 3 possible samples.
solution.why: All pairs are equally likely and every distinct pair has positive joint inclusion probability.
The joint probability is smaller than the product of first-order probabilities under sampling without replacement.

solution.say: For sample {1,2}, the two weighted values are 15 and 30.
solution.why: The off-diagonal product appears twice in the double sum.

ask.q: Why does the off-diagonal contribution appear twice for a two-unit sample?
ask.nudge: The variance formula sums over ordered pairs (i,j), including both (1,2) and (2,1).

scenes.title: Six statements that expose common errors
scenes.objective: Separate estimator properties from variance-estimator properties.
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false, then inspect the reason.

items.claim: The HT estimator of a total is Σᵢ∈s yᵢ/πᵢ.
items.why: Each observed value is weighted by the reciprocal of its first-order inclusion probability.

items.claim: If πᵢ>0 for every unit, the usual unbiased variance estimator is always available.
items.why: The variance estimator also requires the relevant second-order inclusion probabilities πᵢⱼ to be positive.

items.claim: A design-unbiased estimator must equal the population total for every realised sample.
items.why: Unbiasedness concerns the expectation over repeated samples, not each individual outcome.

items.claim: The HT estimator of the population mean is Ŷ_HT/N when N is known.
items.why: The total estimate is divided by the known population size, not by the sample size.

items.claim: An unbiased estimator of a variance can be negative for some samples.
items.why: Unbiasedness is an expectation property; it does not force every realised value to be nonnegative.

items.claim: The second-order inclusion probability is the probability that two specified units are both selected.
items.why: πᵢⱼ records joint inclusion and enters the design variance expression.

scenes.title: Transfer: detect a zero pairwise probability
scenes.objective: Choose the correct inferential conclusion for a design with a never-observed pair.
scenes.problem: A fixed-size design has π₁=π₂=π₃=1/2, but units 1 and 2 are never selected together, so π₁₂=0. What can you conclude about HT estimation of the total and the usual unbiased HT variance estimator?
hints: Check the first-order positivity condition separately from the second-order condition.
Recall which probability appears in the denominator of the variance estimator.
State what remains valid and what is not available; do not infer that both procedures fail.
scenes.answer: The HT total can be design-unbiased because all first-order inclusion probabilities are positive. The usual unbiased HT variance estimator is not available for the pair (1,2), because it requires division by π₁₂=0.
scenes.check: Do not say that the HT total becomes biased. The zero pairwise probability is a variance-estimation limitation, not a failure of the first-order HT unbiasedness proof.

solution.say: The HT total uses first-order probabilities only.
solution.why: Every population unit has a positive chance of appearing, so the HT total is defined and design-unbiased.

solution.say: The usual variance estimator uses pairwise probabilities in its denominator.
solution.why: A pair that never appears cannot contribute an observable sample term to this estimator.

solution.math: HT total: design-unbiased. Usual unbiased HT variance estimator: unavailable for this design.
solution.why: The two procedures require different positivity conditions.

ask.q: Which positivity condition fails in this transfer case?
ask.nudge: It concerns the joint inclusion of two distinct units, not the inclusion of each unit separately.

scenes.title: The exam-ready method
body: Define πᵢ=Pₚ(i∈s). The Horvitz–Thompson total is Ŷ_HT=Σᵢ∈s yᵢ/πᵢ. If every πᵢ>0, its design expectation is Y.
For the mean, divide the HT total by N. Do not divide by n. A realised HT estimate can differ from Y; unbiasedness is about the design average.
Variance uses πᵢⱼ=Pₚ(i,j∈s). The usual unbiased variance estimator divides by πᵢⱼ, so relevant pairwise probabilities must be positive.
Remember three separate claims: the HT total can be unbiased; its variance is nonnegative; an unbiased estimator of that variance can be negative for a realised sample.

scenes.title: Mastery test
scenes.objective: Check independent use of the estimator and its conditions.

sheet: HT mean: ȳ_HT=Ŷ_HT/N when N is known.
Usual unbiased variance estimator requires relevant πᵢⱼ>0.
A single realised estimate need not equal the target.
An unbiased variance estimator may be negative for a realised sample.
cards: Chance that one specified unit is selected
Chance that two specified units are selected together
Divide HT total by known N
Expectation over the design equals the fixed total
Check πᵢⱼ>0 for all required pairs
The estimator is a rule; the estimate is its realised value
Possible for an unbiased estimator, although true variance is ≥0
tricks: Write the target first: total or mean. This prevents an accidental division by n.
For unbiasedness, replace Eₚ(Iᵢ) by πᵢ and cancel the same πᵢ.
Before using a variance estimator, make a separate πᵢⱼ positivity check.
shortcuts: For equal-probability SRS, πᵢ=n/N and the HT total becomes Nȳ_s.
For SRSWOR, πᵢⱼ=n(n−1)/[N(N−1)] for distinct units.
A fixed-size design has Σᵢπᵢ=n; this is a useful probability check.
remember: Positive first-order probabilities support the HT total; positive pairwise probabilities are an additional variance-estimation requirement.
Do not confuse a nonnegative true variance with a necessarily nonnegative unbiased estimate of it.
